doc.title: John Fedchock interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 28, 2015

title: What he thinks about when improvising
summary: He describes shaping lines by harmony, voice leading and tension and release.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: That’s pretty complex. And I wonder if you can tell me what you’re thinking about when you improvise.

First and foremost I’m thinking about the line — the melody that I’m playing. That it’s informed by the harmony, but it also has the direction that the harmony wants it to go. The voice leading in the line, the direction of the resolution of the chords, it all makes sense within that. You know? So if I’m playing a line and I cross into a bar line it’s almost like you can hear the key signature change when you cross into that new chord. And it’s usually by some relationship of a half-step or some kind of resolving note like a seventh resolving into a third, or a third resolving to a seventh, or a sharp nine resolving into a thirteen, or something — like from the different stratas of resolution. So I’m trying to keep that in mind but at the same time I want to create a line that if I create tension in the line somewhere I always want to make sure that that tension is somewhere along the line readdressed and released. And that it’s not necessarily a completely cognizant thing at this point in the way I play. It’s something that I just hear and I know it’s gotta go a certain way. And there may be two or three steps in between here and here. But eventually it ends up — you know like I’ll play some kind of note that sticks out and then I go down here, I’m not going to leave it hanging. I’ll eventually go back up and pick it up and move back in. That’s just kind of — regardless of how much I alter the harmony © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-

or what kind of chord substitutions I use, I’m always trying to think about these tension notes. They’re there for a reason. You know just to play tension notes just for the sake of tension, the great thing about music is tension and release. So they all serve a purpose. Like that seventh — there’s a strong pull to go to the third, on a five-one relationship. So the same thing goes for a lot with the upper extensions. I feel there’s a very strong resolution to a lot of these things. So even if I’m not consciously thinking of it, now I’m to the point where I’m subconsciously remembering that note and coming back up to take care of whatever I left hanging.
I really like that. And you sort of, I think, answered my next question, was about wrong notes in improvising. I think you sort of just addressed it already.
